more_info.overview: Vegetable carbon is a finely divided carbon pigment produced by carbonising plant material and subsequently purifying the powder. It is used to add colour or restore colour lost during food manufacture. Plant material is carbonised and the resulting carbon is purified. Permitted starting materials include wood and other cellulosic material, peat and nut shells. The specified material is supplied as black powder. The specification describes it as effectively insoluble in water.
more_info.uses:
Examples in the EU food-use list include certain other confectionery including breath freshening microsweets; chewing gum; decorations, coatings and fillings, except fruit-based fillings covered by category 4.2.4; flavoured drinks; flavoured fermented milk products including heat-treated products; unripened cheese excluding products falling in category 16.
The entries apply to particular food categories and may limit the amount, the preparation or the way it is used; they do not show how often the additive appears in retail products.
more_info.daily_intake: No ADI allocated (JECFA, 1987); EFSA also could not derive an ADI in 2012.
more_info.origin: Plant material is carbonised and the resulting carbon is purified. Permitted starting materials include wood and other cellulosic material, peat and nut shells.
more_info.dietary_restrictions: The specified starting material is plant derived and compatible with vegetarian and vegan diets. The specification does not establish halal or kosher certification.
more_info.side_effects:
At reported food-use levels, EFSA found no concern for material meeting its stated low-PAH condition.
Available toxicology was too limited for an ADI; contamination is a specific uncertainty.
